title: Luigi’s mansion and the art of chunking
author: Jo Castelino
summary: Castelino, a self-described non-gamer, uses her experience of Luigi's Mansion 3 to illustrate cognitive principles she values in teaching. The game introduces small pieces of procedural knowledge slowly, requires mastery before moving on, and then asks players to apply each skill in new contexts of increasing complexity. Its indirect hints give just enough support to restart thinking without giving the answer. She maps this onto science teaching, where novices face heavy vocabulary and concepts that depend on prior knowledge. Her prescription is careful chunking, plenty of practice, retrieval, and application questions that 'change the scene', with hints faded gradually until students can answer without cues.
points: Good games and good teaching both introduce small skills, ensure mastery, then raise complexity.
Chunking new content protects novices from overload and builds the confidence needed to keep learning.
Retrieval and application in changed contexts, such as moving from plant cell structure to root function, turn mastered facts into transferable knowledge.
Hints should be indirect and gradually withdrawn so students eventually answer without cues.
quotes: The game introduced little ‘skills’ slowly, ensured I mastered them and then made me apply them to different contexts, increasing the complexity each time. The reason I put the word skills in quote marks is because I think of them more as procedural knowledge or, in other words, how to do something in the game.

Another great feature is the hints we receive from E. Gadd (as annoying as he is). If we appear to be stuck, E. Gadd phones Luigi and gives him a small hint to help him on his way. These hints are not direct, but are enough to light a spark in my brain to tell me what I need to do next.

Science (or any other subject) can be daunting to a novice entering our classrooms. There is so much content, a LOT of new words, and difficult concepts that only make sense when prior knowledge is robust.

Chunking new information carefully and guiding our students till they have mastered each bit well is absolutely vital to give our students the confidence to continue learning, develop their schemas and discuss the subject knowledgably. Add to this a lot of practice as well and our students have a chance of committing each piece of information to their long-term memory, which they can then call upon each time it is needed.

Remembering facts is important but we also want our students to apply this knowledge to different contexts, much like I have to on different floors of Luigi’s Mansion. Once students have mastered key information, the next step would be to encourage retrieval and application by providing a lot of questions that ‘change the scene’.

Obviously, to achieve true mastery, we need to ensure students can answer questions without cues and hints but reaching this phase should be gradual. Again, very much like on the game when, earlier on, I had a lot of hints about how to use the Poltergust effectively but by floor 12, I was using it and the Strobulb and jumping and did it all upside down (okay, that last bit is not true…).
